title: The Synoptic Problem
welcome_lead: Compare Matthew, Mark and Luke side by side and confront the puzzle of their literary relations.
meta_desc: A-Level New Testament Studies adventure on the Synoptic Problem: the Two-Source Hypothesis, Q, and the Farrer alternative.
final_note: You have grasped the major solutions to the Synoptic Problem and the role of hypothetical sources.

concepts.def: Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be 'seen together' due to their parallel material.
The dominant scholarly view that Mark was written first and used by Matthew and Luke.
A hypothetical sayings document, from German Quelle ('source'), accounting for non-Markan material shared by Matthew and Luke.
The theory that Matthew and Luke independently used Mark and Q.
The view, championed by Austin Farrer and Mark Goodacre, that Luke used Mark and Matthew, dispensing with Q.
The minority view that Matthew was first, Luke used Matthew, and Mark abridged both.

walkthroughs.body_html: Several lines of evidence point to Mark as earliest: Mark is the shortest yet has the most vivid detail in shared pericopes; Matthew and Luke seem to improve Mark's Greek and theology (e.g. softening Mark 6:5 'he could do no mighty work' to Matthew 13:58 'he did not do many mighty works'). The classic statement is B. H. Streeter's The Four Gospels (1924).

Roughly 235 verses appear in Matthew and Luke but not in Mark - the so-called 'double tradition'. These are largely sayings: the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, the Sermon on the Mount/Plain. Streeter posited Q to explain this, plus M (Matthew's special material) and L (Luke's). The IQP and John Kloppenborg have reconstructed Q's strata.

Austin Farrer's 1955 essay 'On Dispensing with Q' and Mark Goodacre's The Case Against Q (2002) argue that if Luke knew Matthew, no Q is needed. They point to 'minor agreements' of Matthew and Luke against Mark as evidence of literary dependence. Defenders of Q reply that Luke's ordering of common material differs too much from Matthew's to suggest direct use.

mcqs.q: What is the problem of evil?
options: If God is all-loving, all-knowing and all-powerful, why does evil and suffering exist? Logically, all four cannot be true together without explanation.
It is the question of whether evil people will go to hell.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.
Substance dualism means men and women are different.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

mcqs.q: What is substance dualism about mind and body?
options: The view (associated with Descartes) that mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance — a non-physical mind interacting with a physical body.
It is the question of whether the devil really exists.
Substance dualism means men and women are different.
Substance dualism is the belief that humans have two personalities.
